facts.claim: Higher-priced instant games are less regressive than lower-priced games.
facts.quote: the empirical results show that higher-priced instant games are less regressive than lower-priced games.

facts.claim: Counties having a higher-percentage of low-income households have higher sales of lower-priced instant games, but differences in the distribution of household income have no significant impact on higher-priced instant sales.
facts.quote: counties having a higher-percentage of low-income households have higher sales of lower-priced instant games, but differences in the distribution of household income have no significant impact on higher-priced instant sales.

facts.claim: Priming low-income participants to perceive their own income as low relative to an implicit standard causes them to be more likely to purchase lottery tickets.
facts.quote: participants were more likely to purchase lottery tickets when they were primed to perceive that their own income was low relative to an implicit standard.

facts.claim: The taxes on all lottery games are regressive, with instant games having the greatest regressivity.
facts.quote: The authors find that the taxes on all lottery games are regressive, with instant games having the greatest regressivity

facts.claim: State lotteries are extremely popular among the poor, who play the most but can least afford to play.
facts.quote: state lotteries are extremely popular, especially among the poor, who play the most but can least afford to play.

facts.claim: Lottery expenditures are linked to income, location of the household, gender, age, education, social class and whether the household has positive betting expenditures.
facts.quote: Lottery expenditures are affected by income, location of the household, gender, age, education, social class and whether the household has positive betting expenditures.

research.angle: While lottery spending is strongly linked to poverty and regressive taxes, the regressivity of instant games varies significantly by price point.
research.verdict: The evidence consistently shows that lower-income individuals participate more in lotteries and face a regressive tax burden, though higher-priced games may be less regressive.
research.caveat: One study notes that the relationship between lottery sales and poverty is an association and does not prove causation.
